Problem 1: Tidyverse — New Zealand

The nzge data were supplied as an RDS file because the original nzelect package has been archived. Candidate and Party votes are kept separate in all calculations.

nzge <- readRDS("data/nzge.rds") |>
  as_tibble()

1(a) Vote count by year and vote type

votes_by_year_type <- nzge |>
  summarise(
    vote_count = sum(votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(election_year, voting_type)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(vote_count))

votes_by_year_type |>
  mutate(vote_count = comma(vote_count)) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Election year", "Vote type", "Vote count"),
    caption = "New Zealand votes by election year and vote type"
  )

1(b) Party shares of the 2014 Candidate vote

candidate_2014 <- nzge |>
  filter(
    election_year == 2014,
    voting_type == "Candidate"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    votes = sum(votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = party
  ) |>
  mutate(proportion = votes / sum(votes)) |>
  arrange(desc(proportion))

candidate_2014 |>
  mutate(
    votes = comma(votes),
    proportion = percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.01)
  ) |>
  kable(

1(c) Winning party by year and vote type

winning_parties <- nzge |>
  summarise(
    votes = sum(votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(election_year, voting_type, party)
  ) |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = votes,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = TRUE,
    by = c(election_year, voting_type)
  ) |>
  select(election_year, voting_type, party) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = voting_type,
    values_from = party,
    names_glue = "{voting_type}_vote_winner"
  ) |>
  arrange(election_year)

winning_parties |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Election year", "Candidate-vote winner",
                  "Party-vote winner"),
    caption = "Winning party for each vote type"
  )
Winning party for each vote type
Election year Candidate-vote winner Party-vote winner
2002 Labour Party Labour Party
2005 Labour Party National Party
2008 National Party National Party
2011 National Party National Party
2014 National Party National Party

Labour won both vote types in 2002. In 2005, National won the Candidate vote while Labour won the Party vote. National won both vote types in 2008, 2011, and 2014.

Problem 2: Tidyverse — Tennis

The 2019 ATP match data come from the assigned Tennis Abstract repository. Each row is one match; the file contains separate winner and loser columns.

matches <- read_csv(
  "data/atp_matches_2019.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

2(b) Players winning multiple tournaments

A tournament champion is identified as the winner of a match whose round is coded F (final).

tournament_titles <- matches |>
  filter(round == "F") |>
  count(winner_name, name = "tournaments_won", sort = TRUE)

multiple_title_winners <- tournament_titles |>
  filter(tournaments_won > 1)

multiple_title_winners |>

    col.names = c("Player", "Tournaments won"),
    caption = "Players who won more than one tournament"

2(c) Do winners have more aces?

Because both ace totals come from the same match, I analyze the within-match difference, winner aces minus loser aces. Matches missing either ace count are excluded.

ace_differences <- matches |>
  filter(!is.na(w_ace), !is.na(l_ace)) |>
  transmute(ace_difference = w_ace - l_ace)

ace_summary <- ace_differences |>
  summarise(
    matches = n(),
    mean_difference = mean(ace_difference),
    median_difference = median(ace_difference),
    winner_had_more = mean(ace_difference > 0)
  )

ace_summary |>
  mutate(winner_had_more = percent(winner_had_more, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Complete matches", "Mean difference",
                  "Median difference", "Winner had more aces"),
    caption = "Within-match ace comparison"
  )
Within-match ace comparison
Complete matches Mean difference Median difference Winner had more aces
2694 1.7 1 57.3%

I use a one-sided, simulation-based test from the infer package. The null hypothesis is that the population mean difference is zero, against the alternative that it is positive. This keeps the inferential workflow in the tidyverse rather than calling a base-R hypothesis-test function.

set.seed(506)

observed_ace_mean <- ace_differences |>
  specify(response = ace_difference) |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

null_ace_distribution <- ace_differences |>
  specify(response = ace_difference) |>
  hypothesize(null = "point", mu = 0) |>
  generate(reps = 9999, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "mean")

ace_test <- null_ace_distribution |>
  summarise(
    p_value =
      (sum(stat >= observed_ace_mean$stat) + 1) / (n() + 1)
  )

tibble(
  observed_mean_difference = observed_ace_mean$stat,
  simulation_p_value = ace_test$p_value
) |>
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    col.names = c("Observed mean difference", "One-sided p-value"),
    caption = "Simulation-based test of winner-minus-loser aces"
  )
Simulation-based test of winner-minus-loser aces
Observed mean difference One-sided p-value
1.7049 1e-04

Winners averaged 1.7 more aces per match. The one-sided simulation p-value is <0.001. This is strong evidence that winners have more aces than losers on average. This is an association within completed matches; it does not establish that aces alone cause a player to win.

2(d) Highest win rate, minimum five matches

I reshape winners and losers into a common player column, mark each outcome, and then calculate wins divided by total matches.

player_records <- bind_rows(
  matches |>
    transmute(player = winner_name, won = 1L),
  matches |>
    transmute(player = loser_name, won = 0L)
) |>
  summarise(
    matches = n(),
    wins = sum(won),
    losses = matches - wins,
    win_rate = mean(won),
    .by = player
  ) |>
  filter(matches >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(win_rate), desc(matches))

highest_win_rate <- player_records |>
  slice_max(win_rate, n = 1, with_ties = TRUE)

highest_win_rate |>
  mutate(win_rate = percent(win_rate, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Player", "Matches", "Wins", "Losses", "Win rate"),
    caption = "Highest 2019 win rate among players with at least five matches"
  )
Highest 2019 win rate among players with at least five matches
Player Matches Wins Losses Win rate
Rafael Nadal 69 60 9 87.0%

Rafael Nadal had the highest win rate: 60 wins in 69 matches, or 87.0%.

Problem 3: Visualization — US COVID-19 cases

The data are the assigned New York Times state-level rolling averages. The source already supplies seven-day average daily cases and rates per 100,000 population.

covid <- read_csv("data/us-states.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

3(a) Major and minor spikes

To make “spike” reproducible, I define a peak as a local maximum within a plus-or-minus 28-day window, after summing the state seven-day averages. Peaks below 25,000 cases per day are omitted as small fluctuations. A retained peak is called major when it reaches at least 150,000 daily cases and minor otherwise.

national_cases <- covid |>
  summarise(
    cases_avg = sum(cases_avg, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = date
  ) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(
    local_window_max = slide_dbl(
      cases_avg,
      max,
      .before = 28,
      .after = 28,
      .complete = TRUE
    )
  )

case_peaks <- national_cases |>
  filter(
    cases_avg == local_window_max,
    cases_avg >= 25000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    spike_type = if_else(cases_avg >= 150000, "Major", "Minor"),
    label = str_c(format(date, "%b %Y"), "\n", comma(round(cases_avg)))
  )

spike_counts <- case_peaks |>
  count(spike_type, name = "number_of_spikes")

spike_counts |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Spike classification", "Number of spikes"),
    caption = "Detected national COVID-19 case spikes"
  )
Detected national COVID-19 case spikes
Spike classification Number of spikes
Major 3
Minor 5 
ggplot(national_cases, aes(date, cases_avg)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#9ecae1", alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_line(color = "#08519c", linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_point(
    data = case_peaks,
    aes(color = spike_type),
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = case_peaks,
    aes(label = label, color = spike_type),
    size = 2.7,
    linewidth = 0.15,
    fill = "white",
    nudge_y = 36000,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Major = "#b2182b", Minor = "#ef8a62")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Eight distinct US COVID-19 case spikes",
    subtitle = "Three peaks meet the ≥150,000 major-spike threshold; five are minor",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Seven-day average daily cases",
    color = "Spike type",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times COVID-19 data; local maxima use a ±28-day window."
  )

Under this definition, there are 3 major spikes and 5 minor spikes. The January 2022 Omicron peak is visually exceptional at more than 800,000 average daily cases, over three times the next-largest peak.

3(b) Highest- and lowest-rate states

I restrict “states” to the 50 states plus the District of Columbia. Summing the daily cases_avg_per_100k values across the full period gives an approximately cumulative, population-standardized rate and permits a fair ranking across states of different sizes.

states_50_dc <- c(state.name, "District of Columbia")

overall_state_rates <- covid |>
  filter(state %in% states_50_dc) |>
  summarise(
    overall_rate = sum(cases_avg_per_100k, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = state
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(overall_rate))

extreme_states <- bind_rows(
  overall_state_rates |> slice_head(n = 1) |> mutate(rank = "Highest"),
  overall_state_rates |> slice_tail(n = 1) |> mutate(rank = "Lowest")
)

extreme_states |>
  mutate(overall_rate = comma(overall_rate, accuracy = 1)) |>
  select(rank, state, overall_rate) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Overall-rate rank", "State",
                  "Summed daily rate per 100,000"),
    caption = "States at the extremes of the overall population-standardized rate"
  )
States at the extremes of the overall population-standardized rate
Overall-rate rank State Summed daily rate per 100,000
Highest Rhode Island 43,296
Lowest Maine 22,020 
extreme_trajectories <- covid |>
  filter(state %in% extreme_states$state)

ggplot(
  extreme_trajectories,
  aes(date, cases_avg_per_100k, color = state)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Maine" = "#2c7fb8", "Rhode Island" = "#d7301f")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number()) +
  labs(
    title = "Rhode Island's waves were far sharper than Maine's",
    subtitle = "Daily new cases per 100,000 residents, seven-day average",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Cases per 100,000",
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Source: The New York Times COVID-19 data."
  )

Rhode Island has the highest overall standardized rate, while Maine has the lowest. Rhode Island experienced much larger winter surges, especially the Omicron wave, which peaked above 500 cases per 100,000 per day. Maine’s curve was lower and flatter early in the pandemic, and its recorded peak was only about 81 per 100,000. The gap is therefore driven not just by one date but by repeatedly higher and sharper Rhode Island waves.

3(c) First five states substantially affected

I define “substantial” as the first date a state’s seven-day average reached 5 new daily cases per 100,000. This threshold is high enough to avoid labeling isolated initial cases as sustained community spread. Territories are excluded using the same 50-state-plus-DC definition.

first_substantial_dates <- covid |>
  filter(
    state %in% states_50_dc,
    cases_avg_per_100k >= 5
  ) |>
  summarise(
    first_substantial = min(date),
    .by = state
  ) |>
  arrange(first_substantial) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

first_substantial_dates |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("State", "First date at or above 5 per 100,000"),
    caption = "First five states to cross the substantial-spread threshold"
  )
First five states to cross the substantial-spread threshold
State First date at or above 5 per 100,000
New York 2020-03-21
New Jersey 2020-03-24
Louisiana 2020-03-26
Massachusetts 2020-03-27
Michigan 2020-03-28 
early_trajectories <- covid |>
  filter(
    state %in% first_substantial_dates$state,
    between(date, as.Date("2020-03-01"), as.Date("2020-05-31"))
  )

ggplot(early_trajectories, aes(date, cases_avg_per_100k)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, color = "#636363", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = "#2b8cbe", linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(
    data = first_substantial_dates,
    aes(xintercept = first_substantial),
    color = "#d7301f",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = first_substantial_dates,
    aes(x = first_substantial, y = 5),
    color = "#d7301f",
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ state, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(
    title = "The Northeast led the first wave of substantial state-level spread",
    subtitle = "Red markers show the first date the 7-day average reached 5 cases per 100,000",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Daily cases per 100,000",
    caption = "Source: The New York Times COVID-19 data. Scales vary by panel to reveal timing."
  ) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )

The first five states were New York (March 21), New Jersey (March 24), Louisiana (March 26), Massachusetts (March 27), and Michigan (March 28). Four of the five are in the Northeast/Midwest corridor, supporting the argument that the first large US wave was geographically concentrated there, with Louisiana as the notable early Southern exception.
